steps.title: Your first HTML element
body:
HTML describes the content of a page using **elements**. Most elements have an opening tag like `

`, some content, and a closing tag with a slash like `

`.
`<h1>` is the biggest heading on a page. Browsers show it large and bold. The preview on the right updates as you type.

steps.title: Paragraphs
body:
The `

` element holds a paragraph of text. Browsers add a little space above and below each paragraph automatically.
Elements are written in the order they appear on the page, top to bottom.

steps.title: Sub-headings
body: Headings go from `<h1>` (most important) down to `<h6>`. Use one `<h1>` per page, then `<h2>` for sections, `<h3>` for sub-sections, and so on.
Search engines and screen readers use headings to understand how your page is organised, so pick them by meaning, not by size.

steps.title: Emphasis: strong and em
body: Inside text you can mark words as important with `<strong>` (shown in bold) or emphasised with `<em>` (shown in italics).
These are **inline** elements: they sit inside a line of text instead of starting a new block.

steps.title: Lists
body: An unordered (bulleted) list is a `<ul>` element containing one `<li>` (list item) per bullet. Use `<ol>` instead for a numbered list.
Elements inside other elements are called **children**. Indenting children makes your HTML much easier to read.

steps.title: Images and alt text
body: `` shows an image. It has no closing tag. `src` is the image's address and `alt` describes it for people using screen readers, and for everyone when the image fails to load.
Good alt text says what matters about the picture in a few words. It's not optional: it's how a large part of the web's audience experiences images.

steps.title: Group content with main
body: Semantic elements describe *what* a region is. `<main>` wraps the main content of a page; `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<section>` and `<footer>` mark other regions.
They don't change how things look, but they help screen readers, search engines and other developers.

steps.title: A complete HTML document
body: Real pages have a skeleton: `<!DOCTYPE html>` on the first line, then `<html>` containing a `<head>` (information about the page) and a `<body>` (what you see).
The `<title>` in the head is the text shown on the browser tab and in search results.
steps.task: Turn your code into a full document: add `<!DOCTYPE html>`, `<html>`, a `<head>` with a `<title>`, and put your `<main>` inside `<body>`. You can delete the comment.

body: CSS styles HTML. A **rule** has a selector (which elements), then properties in braces: `h1 { color: tomato; }`.

steps.title: Classes and the box model
body: A **class** lets you style chosen elements: add `class="card"` in the HTML and target it in CSS with a dot, `.card { … }`.
Every element is a box: content, then **padding** (space inside the border), then the border, then **margin** (space outside). `border-radius` rounds the corners.

courses.title: Python from Zero
courses.tagline: Your first programming language, one idea at a time.
courses.desc: The friendliest place to start. Print, store values, make decisions, repeat with loops and write functions, all while building a small grade-report program.

steps.title: Hello, world!
body: A program is a list of instructions the computer runs from top to bottom. In Python, `print()` shows something on the screen.
Text in code is called a **string** and goes inside quotes. Press **Check your code** (or Ctrl/⌘ + Enter) to run your program and see the output.
steps.task: Write a line that prints exactly `Hello, world!`
steps.solution: print("Hello, world!")
steps.hint: `print("Hello, world!")` — mind the capital H, the comma and the exclamation mark.

steps.title: Several lines
body: Each `print()` call prints one line. Python runs them in order.
A line starting with `#` is a **comment**. Python ignores it; it's a note for humans.
steps.task: Below your first line, add two more `print()` calls: one with your name and one with why you're learning to code.

tests.msg: Your program prints at least three lines.

steps.title: Python is a calculator
body: Python does maths with `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide). Numbers don't need quotes.
`print(2 + 3)` prints `5`, but `print("2 + 3")` prints the text `2 + 3`. Quotes make all the difference.

steps.title: Variables
body: A **variable** is a name for a value: `student = "Ada"`. The `=` means *store this value under this name*, not *is equal to*.
After that, use the name anywhere you'd use the value: `print(student)`.

steps.title: Numbers in variables
body: Variables can hold numbers too. Integers like `88` are written without quotes.
You can combine variables in expressions: `total = a + b + c` adds them and stores the result.

steps.title: Division and rounding
body: `/` always gives a decimal number (a **float**): `7 / 2` is `3.5`.
`round(x, 1)` rounds to one decimal place: `round(86.333, 1)` is `86.3`.

steps.title: Decisions with if / elif / else
body: `if` runs a block only when a condition is true. Indent the block with 4 spaces; the indentation is how Python knows what's inside.
`elif` (else if) checks the next condition only when the previous ones were false; `else` catches everything left.

courses.title: JavaScript from Zero
courses.desc: Variables, decisions, arrays, functions and objects, then the modern trio of map, filter and reduce, by building a café order calculator that prints a receipt.
courses.project: a café order calculator with receipts

steps.title: Hello, JavaScript
body: JavaScript is the language of the web: every browser runs it. `console.log()` prints a value to the console (the output panel).
Statements usually end with a semicolon `;`.
steps.task: Print exactly `Hello, JavaScript!`
steps.solution: console.log("Hello, JavaScript!");

steps.title: const and let
body: `const` creates a variable that can't be reassigned. `let` creates one that can.
Default to `const`; use `let` only when the value must change.
steps.task: Create `const shop = "Code Café";` and `let items = 0;` then print `shop`.

steps.title: Numbers and maths
body: JavaScript has one number type for integers and decimals. Use `+ - * /` and `%` (remainder).
Decimals can surprise you: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, because computers store numbers in binary. That's why shops often count in cents.
steps.task: Create `const price = 4.5;` and `const qty = 3;` then print `price * qty`.

steps.title: Template literals
body: Backtick strings can embed values: `` `Total: ${price * qty}` ``. Anything inside `${ }` is evaluated.
They can also span several lines, which is handy for building text.
steps.task: Print exactly `3 coffees cost $13.5` using a template literal with `qty` and `price * qty`.

steps.title: if / else
body: `if (condition) { … } else { … }` chooses a branch. Comparisons: `===` (equal), `!==`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.
Always use `===` rather than `==`: the double version converts types in surprising ways (`0 == ""` is true!).
steps.task: Create `const total = price * qty;` and `let shipping;`. If `total >= 20`, set `shipping` to 0, otherwise 5. Print `shipping`.

steps.title: The ternary operator
body: `condition ? a : b` is a compact if/else that produces a value.
Great for simple choices; use a full `if` when either branch gets long.
steps.task: Create `const freeShipping = total >= 20 ? "yes" : "no";` and print it.

steps.title: Arrays
body: An **array** is an ordered list: `const cart = [4.5, 3.25, 6];`. Indexes start at 0.
`cart.length` is the number of items, and `cart.push(x)` adds one to the end.
steps.task: Create `const cart = [4.5, 3.25, 6];` and print its length.

steps.title: Loops: for...of
body: `for (const item of cart) { … }` runs once per item.
Combine it with an accumulator to total things up.
steps.task: Create `let sum = 0;` and use a `for...of` loop to add every price in `cart` to `sum`. Print `sum`.

steps.title: Functions
body: `function addTax(amount) { return amount * 1.1; }` defines a reusable function. `return` gives back the result.
Calling `addTax(10)` returns `11.000000000000002`. Floating point again, which is why money code rounds.
steps.task: Define `function addTax(amount)` that returns the amount plus 10% tax.

steps.title: Arrow functions
body: Arrow functions are a shorter syntax: `const double = n => n * 2;`. With two parameters, use parentheses: `(a, b) => a + b`.
You'll see them everywhere in modern JavaScript, especially with array methods.
steps.task: Create `const discount = (amount, pct) => …` that returns the amount reduced by `pct` percent.

steps.title: Objects
body: An **object** groups related values under named keys: `{ name: "Latte", price: 4.5 }`.
Read a value with a dot: `item.name`.
steps.task: Create `const item = { name: "Latte", price: 4.5, qty: 2 };` and print `item.name`.

tests.msg: `item` has the right name, price and qty.

steps.title: An array of objects
body: Real data is usually a list of objects, one per thing: users, products, orders.
This shape is exactly what JSON from a web API looks like.
steps.task: Create `order`: an array of three objects: Latte (4.5, qty 2), Bagel (3.25, qty 1) and Juice (6, qty 1), each with `name`, `price` and `qty`.

tests.msg: The first item is two Lattes.

steps.title: map: transform every item
body: `array.map(fn)` returns a **new** array with `fn` applied to each item. The original is unchanged.
`order.map(i => i.name)` gives `["Latte", "Bagel", "Juice"]`.
steps.task: Create `lineTotals` with `map`: each item's `price * qty`.

steps.title: filter: keep some items
body: `array.filter(fn)` keeps the items for which `fn` returns true.
Chaining `filter` then `map` reads like a sentence: keep these, then transform them.
steps.task: Create `pricey`: the items in `order` whose `price` is more than 4.

steps.title: reduce: combine into one value
body: `array.reduce((acc, item) => …, start)` walks the array carrying an accumulator. It's the functional version of the loop-and-add pattern.
Always pass the starting value (here `0`); it avoids a crash on empty arrays.
steps.task: Create `orderTotal` using `reduce`: the sum of `price * qty` over the whole order.

steps.title: Print a receipt
body: Put it all together: a function that takes data and returns a formatted string.
`array.join("\n")` glues strings together with newlines between them.
steps.task: Write `function receipt(order)` that returns one line per item like `Latte x2 = 9`, then a final line `Total: 18.25`. Print `receipt(order)`.

tests.msg: The receipt has the line `Latte x2 = 9`.
It works for any order, not just this one.

courses.title: SQL from Zero
courses.schema:
movies(id, title, year, genre, score, director_id)
directors(id, name, country)
courses.tagline: Ask questions of data. Every app has a database.
courses.desc: Query a real SQLite database of films and directors: filter, sort, count, group, join tables and change data safely. The most useful skill in tech that isn't a programming language.

steps.title: SELECT everything
body: A database stores data in **tables**: rows (records) and columns (fields). SQL is the language for asking questions of it.
`SELECT * FROM movies;` returns every column (`*`) of every row in the `movies` table.
steps.task: Select every column from the `movies` table.
steps.solution: SELECT * FROM movies;

tests.msg: Your query returns all 13 movies with every column.

steps.title: Choose columns
body: List the columns you want, separated by commas, instead of `*`. Asking only for what you need is faster and clearer.
Column names come back in the order you list them.
steps.task: Select just the `title` and `year` of every movie.
steps.solution: SELECT title, year FROM movies;

tests.msg: The result has exactly the columns `title` and `year`.

steps.title: Filter with WHERE
body: `WHERE` keeps only rows that match a condition: `WHERE year > 2015`.
Text values go in single quotes: `WHERE genre = 'Drama'`.
steps.task: Select the `title` of every movie released **after 2015**.
steps.solution: SELECT title FROM movies WHERE year > 2015;

tests.msg: You get exactly the movies after 2015.

steps.title: AND and OR
body: Combine conditions with `AND` (both must be true) and `OR` (either).
Use parentheses when you mix them, so the meaning is unambiguous.
steps.task: Select the `title` and `score` of **Sci-Fi** movies with a score of **at least 8.0**.
steps.solution: SELECT title, score FROM movies WHERE genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND score >= 8.0;

tests.msg: You get exactly the Sci-Fi movies scoring 8.0 or more.

steps.title: Sort with ORDER BY
body: `ORDER BY score DESC` sorts from highest to lowest; `ASC` (the default) sorts lowest first.
Without ORDER BY, a database may return rows in any order. Never rely on it.
steps.task: Select `title` and `score` for all movies, highest score first.
steps.solution: SELECT title, score FROM movies ORDER BY score DESC;

tests.msg: All movies appear, sorted by score from high to low.

steps.title: Top N with LIMIT
body: `LIMIT 3` keeps only the first three rows of the result.
Combined with ORDER BY, it answers every 'top N' question.
steps.task: Select the `title` of the **3 highest-scoring** movies.
steps.solution: SELECT title FROM movies ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 3;

tests.msg: You get the top three titles, best first.

steps.title: Count rows
body: **Aggregate functions** summarise many rows into one: `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(col)`, `AVG(col)`, `MIN(col)`, `MAX(col)`.
`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM movies WHERE …` counts matching rows.
steps.task: Count how many movies are in the **Drama** genre.
steps.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM movies WHERE genre = 'Drama';

steps.title: Group with GROUP BY
body: `GROUP BY genre` splits rows into one group per genre; aggregates then run once per group.
Every selected column must either be in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.
steps.task: For each `genre`, show the genre and how many movies it has.
steps.solution: SELECT genre, COUNT(*) FROM movies GROUP BY genre;

tests.msg: One row per genre with the right counts.

steps.title: Averages and aliases
body: `AVG(score)` averages a column. `ROUND(x, 2)` rounds to two decimals.
`AS` gives a result column a readable name: `ROUND(AVG(score), 2) AS avg_score`.
steps.task: For each `genre`, show the genre and its average score rounded to 2 decimals, named `avg_score`.
steps.solution: SELECT genre, ROUND(AVG(score), 2) AS avg_score FROM movies GROUP BY genre;

tests.msg: Each genre's rounded average is correct.

steps.title: Filter groups with HAVING
body: `WHERE` filters rows **before** grouping; `HAVING` filters groups **after** aggregating.
So 'genres with more than 2 movies' needs `HAVING COUNT(*) > 2`.
steps.task: Show each `genre` that has **more than 2** movies, with its count.
steps.solution: SELECT genre, COUNT(*) FROM movies GROUP BY genre HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

tests.msg: Only genres with more than two movies appear.

steps.title: JOIN two tables
body: Movies store a `director_id`, not the director's name. That avoids repeating data. A **JOIN** puts it back together.
`FROM movies JOIN directors ON movies.director_id = directors.id` pairs each movie with its director's row.
steps.task: Show each movie's `title` with its director's `name`.
steps.solution: SELECT movies.title, directors.name FROM movies JOIN directors ON movies.director_id = directors.id;

tests.msg: Every movie appears with its director's name.

steps.title: JOIN + GROUP BY
body: Joins and aggregates combine naturally: join first, then group by a column from either table.
This is the heart of analytics queries.
steps.task: Show each director's `name` and the number of movies they directed.
steps.solution: SELECT directors.name, COUNT(*) FROM movies JOIN directors ON movies.director_id = directors.id GROUP BY directors.name;

tests.msg: Each director appears with the right count.

steps.title: INSERT a row
body: `INSERT INTO movies (title, year, genre, score, director_id) VALUES (...)` adds a row. The `id` fills itself in.
Each run starts from a fresh copy of the database, so experiment freely.
steps.task: Insert Christopher Nolan's **Tenet** (2020, genre `Action`, score 7.3, `director_id` 1). Then run `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM movies;` to prove there are now 14.
steps.solution:
INSERT INTO movies (title, year, genre, score, director_id) VALUES ('Tenet', 2020, 'Action', 7.3, 1);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM movies;
steps.hint: Two statements, each ending in a semicolon: the INSERT, then the SELECT.

steps.title: UPDATE carefully
body: `UPDATE movies SET score = 9.1 WHERE title = 'Arrival';` changes matching rows.
**Always** write the WHERE first. An UPDATE without WHERE changes every row in the table.
steps.task: Set Arrival's score to `8.2`, then select the `title` and `score` of Arrival to confirm.
steps.solution:
UPDATE movies SET score = 8.2 WHERE title = 'Arrival';
SELECT title, score FROM movies WHERE title = 'Arrival';

steps.title: Subqueries
body: A query can contain another query in parentheses. `(SELECT AVG(score) FROM movies)` evaluates to a single number you can compare against.
Subqueries let you answer two-step questions in one statement.
steps.task: Select the `title` of every movie that scores **above the average** score of all movies.
steps.solution: SELECT title FROM movies WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM movies);

tests.msg: You get exactly the above-average movies.

body: Real data is usually a **list of records**. In Python each record is a dictionary, so a whole table is a list of dicts.

courses.title: SQL Analytics
courses.schema:
customers(id, name, city)
products(id, name, category, price)
orders(id, customer_id, order_date)
order_items(order_id, product_id, qty)
courses.tagline: Joins, CTEs and window functions on a shop's data.
courses.desc: The SQL that analysts and backend developers use every day. Join four tables, group and filter, label rows with CASE, then write CTEs and window functions for rankings, running totals and month-over-month change. Take SQL from Zero first.
courses.project: a sales report for an online shop

steps.title: Join two tables
body: Data is split across tables so nothing is stored twice: an order holds a `customer_id`, not the customer's name. A **JOIN** puts them back together.
`FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id` pairs each order with its customer. `o` and `c` are short **aliases**.
steps.task: Select each order's `id`, its `order_date` and the customer's `name`.
steps.solution: SELECT o.id, o.order_date, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;

tests.msg: Every order is listed with its customer's name.

steps.title: LEFT JOIN: find what's missing
body: A plain `JOIN` drops rows with no match. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with `NULL` when nothing matches.
So `WHERE o.id IS NULL` after a `LEFT JOIN` finds customers who never ordered. (Use `IS NULL`, never `= NULL`.)
steps.task: Select the `name` of every customer who has never placed an order.
steps.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

tests.msg: You find the one customer with no orders.

steps.title: Three tables and a calculation
body: Joins chain: orders → order_items → products. Each `JOIN … ON …` adds one table.
Columns can be calculated: `oi.qty * p.price AS line_total` names the result.
steps.task: For every row in `order_items`, select the `order_id`, the product `name` and `line_total` (quantity times price).
steps.solution: SELECT oi.order_id, p.name, oi.qty * p.price AS line_total FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id;

tests.msg: Every line has the right total.

steps.title: Revenue by category
body: `GROUP BY` folds rows into one per group, and aggregate functions like `SUM` work across each group.
Combine it with joins and you can answer business questions: which category earns most?
steps.task: Select each product `category` and its total `revenue` (sum of quantity × price), highest revenue first.
steps.solution: SELECT p.category, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS revenue FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.category ORDER BY revenue DESC;

tests.msg: Each category's revenue is correct, highest first.

steps.title: HAVING filters groups
body: `WHERE` filters rows *before* grouping. `HAVING` filters groups *after*, so it can use aggregates: `HAVING SUM(...) > 100`.
steps.task: Select the `name` and `total` spent by every customer who spent **more than 150** in all.
steps.solution: SELECT c.name, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY c.id HAVING total > 150;

tests.msg: You get exactly the customers who spent over 150.

steps.hint: Join customers → orders → order_items → products, group by customer, then `HAVING SUM(oi.qty * p.price) > 150`.

steps.title: CASE: label your data
body: `CASE WHEN condition THEN value … ELSE value END` is SQL's if/else. It creates a new column from rules.
Conditions are checked in order, and the first match wins.
steps.task: Select every product's `name`, `price` and a `band`: `budget` under 10, `mid` under 50, otherwise `premium`.
steps.solution: SELECT name, price, CASE WHEN price < 10 THEN 'budget' WHEN price < 50 THEN 'mid' ELSE 'premium' END AS band FROM products;

tests.msg: Every product has the right band.

steps.title: Grouping by month
body: Dates here are text like `2024-02-14`. SQLite's `strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)` cuts them down to the month, `2024-02`, which you can group by.
Other databases have `DATE_TRUNC` or `EXTRACT`; the idea is the same.
steps.task: Select each `month` and the number of `orders` placed in it, in month order.
steps.solution: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

tests.msg: Each month has the right number of orders, in order.

steps.title: CTEs: name a step
body: A **common table expression** names a query so the next one can use it like a table: `WITH totals AS (SELECT …) SELECT … FROM totals`.
CTEs turn one giant query into readable steps. They're how analysts write SQL in real life.
steps.task: With a CTE `totals` holding each order's id and total, select the average order total as `avg_order`.
steps.solution: WITH totals AS (SELECT oi.order_id, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS total FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY oi.order_id) SELECT AVG(total) AS avg_order FROM totals;

tests.msg: The average order total is correct.

steps.title: Window functions: rank
body: A **window function** calculates across rows without folding them together. `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC)` numbers rows by total, while every row stays in the result.
Compare with `GROUP BY`, which returns one row per group. Windows return one row per row, plus a value computed from its neighbours.
steps.task: Using a CTE of each customer's `name` and `total` spent, select `name`, `total` and `place` (their `RANK()` by total, biggest first), in place order.
steps.solution: WITH spend AS (SELECT c.name, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY c.id) SELECT name, total, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total DESC) AS place FROM spend ORDER BY place;

tests.msg: You used a window function with `OVER`.

steps.title: PARTITION BY: best in each group
body: `PARTITION BY` restarts the window for each group: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC)` ranks products within their own category.
Wrap it in a CTE and keep rank 1 to get the top item per group, a classic analytics question.
steps.task: For each category, select the `category`, product `name` and `units` (total quantity sold) of its best-selling product.
steps.solution: WITH sold AS (SELECT p.category, p.name, SUM(oi.qty) AS units, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY SUM(oi.qty) DESC) AS r FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.id) SELECT category, name, units FROM sold WHERE r = 1;

tests.msg: You get the top product in each category.

steps.hint: Window functions can't go in `WHERE`, so rank inside a CTE and filter `WHERE r = 1` outside it.

steps.title: Running totals
body: `SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY month)` adds up every row so far: a running total. It's how dashboards draw cumulative revenue lines.
steps.task: With a CTE of monthly `revenue`, select `month`, `revenue` and `running` (the running total), in month order.
steps.solution: WITH monthly AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY month) SELECT month, revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running FROM monthly ORDER BY month;

tests.msg: The running total is correct for each month.

steps.title: LAG: compare with last month
body: `LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)` returns the previous row's value (`NULL` for the first row). Subtract it to get month-over-month change.
You can now join, group, label, chain steps with CTEs and use window functions. That's the toolkit of a data analyst.
steps.task: Using the same monthly CTE, select `month`, `revenue` and `change` (revenue minus the previous month's revenue), in month order.
steps.solution: WITH monthly AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month, SUM(oi.qty * p.price) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY month) SELECT month, revenue, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change FROM monthly ORDER BY month;

tests.msg: Each month's change is correct (the first month has none).

courses.title: Algorithms with Python
courses.tagline: Searching, sorting, recursion and Big-O, by measuring them.
courses.desc: Write the classic algorithms yourself and count their steps: linear and binary search, selection and merge sort, recursion, memoisation and breadth-first search through a maze. The bridge from writing code to solving Problems.
courses.project: an algorithm toolkit and a sorting race

steps.title: Linear search
body: An **algorithm** is a precise recipe for solving a problem. The simplest search checks every item in turn until it finds the target.
If the list has n items, the worst case checks all n. We say it takes **O(n)** time: double the list, double the work.
steps.task: Write `linear_search(items, target)` that returns the index of `target`, or `-1` if it isn't there. Print `linear_search([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42], 23)`.

tests.msg: It returns the first index of the target.

steps.title: Binary search
body: If the list is **sorted**, look at the middle item. If the target is bigger, it can only be in the right half; if smaller, the left half. Each step throws away half the list.
1,000,000 items take at most 20 steps. That's **O(log n)**, and it's why sorted data is so valuable.
steps.task: Write `binary_search(items, target)` for a sorted list, returning the index or `-1`. Use `lo` and `hi` indexes and a `while lo <= hi` loop.

tests.py: all(binary_search(list(range(0, 200, 2)), x) == x // 2 for x in range(0, 200, 2))
tests.msg: It finds every item in a sorted list.
It returns -1 for missing items, including an empty list.
It uses a loop, not `index()` or `in`.

steps.hint: `mid = (lo + hi) // 2`. Move `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1` so the range always shrinks.

steps.title: Count the steps
body: Big-O is easier to believe when you measure it. Change each search to also count how many items it looks at.
Return two values at once as a tuple: `return i, steps`.
steps.task: Write `count_linear(items, target)` and `count_binary(items, target)` that return how many comparisons each search makes. On `list(range(1000))` searching for `999`, print both counts.

tests.msg: `count_linear` counts every item it looks at.
`count_binary` needs at most 10 steps for 1,000 items.

steps.title: Recursion
body: A **recursive** function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a **base case** that stops the calls, or it runs forever.
`factorial(5) = 5 × factorial(4)`, down to `factorial(0) = 1`. Many algorithms (merge sort, tree searches) are naturally recursive.
steps.task: Write a recursive `factorial(n)` and a recursive `total(items)` that adds a list by returning `items[0] + total(items[1:])` (an empty list totals 0). Print `factorial(5)`.

steps.title: Selection sort
body: Sorting is the most studied problem in computing. **Selection sort**: find the smallest item, swap it to the front, repeat for the rest.
Two nested loops over n items: **O(n²)**. Simple, but 1,000 items need about 500,000 comparisons.
steps.task: Write `selection_sort(items)` that returns a new sorted list (copy the input first with `items[:]`).

tests.msg: It sorts, including duplicates and empty lists.
It doesn't change the original list.
It doesn't use Python's built-in sorting.

steps.title: Merging sorted lists
body: Two **sorted** lists can be merged in one pass: compare the fronts, take the smaller, repeat. When one list runs out, append the rest of the other.
That's O(n), and it's the key move of merge sort, next.
steps.task: Write `merge(a, b)` that merges two sorted lists into one sorted list.

tests.msg: It handles empty lists and duplicates.

steps.title: Merge sort
body: **Merge sort** splits the list in half, sorts each half (recursively), then merges them. A list of 0 or 1 items is already sorted: the base case.
The list halves log n times and each level does O(n) merging, so it's **O(n log n)**. For 1,000 items that's about 10,000 steps instead of 500,000.
steps.task: Write `merge_sort(items)` using `merge`. Print `merge_sort([38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10])`.

tests.py: (lambda r: merge_sort(r) == sorted(r))([(i * 7919) % 1009 for i in range(500)])

steps.title: Memoisation
body: The naive recursive Fibonacci, `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`, recomputes the same values again and again: `fib(40)` makes over 300 million calls.
**Memoisation** stores each answer the first time, in a dictionary, and reuses it. Each `fib(k)` is computed once, so it's O(n). That's the core idea of dynamic programming.
steps.task: Write `fib(n, memo=None)` with `fib(0) = 0` and `fib(1) = 1` that caches results in a dict. Print `fib(80)`.

tests.msg: The first ten values are right.

steps.hint: Use `memo=None` and create the dict inside, so each top-level call starts fresh. A default of `{}` would be shared between calls.

steps.title: Breadth-first search
body: A maze is a **graph**: each open cell links to its neighbours. **Breadth-first search** explores in rings: everything 1 step away, then 2, and so on, using a queue.
So the first time BFS reaches the exit, it got there in the fewest steps. `collections.deque` gives a fast queue with `popleft()`.
steps.task: Write `shortest_path(maze)` for a list of strings where `#` is a wall, `S` the start and `E` the exit. Return the fewest moves (up, down, left, right) from S to E, or `-1` if there's no way through.

tests.msg: It finds the 14-move path through the example maze.
It handles a neighbouring exit and a blocked one.
It finds the shortest route in an open grid.

steps.title: Race your algorithms
body: Time to see Big-O for real. `time.perf_counter()` reads a precise clock; the difference between two readings is how long the code between them took.
You've written searching, sorting, recursion, memoisation and graph search: the foundations every harder algorithm builds on. The Problems section is the next stop.

tests.msg: Both sorts give the same, correct result.
